1	# Wireless 101 — Module 1: How Wireless Communication Works
2	
3	**Course:** Wireless 101 (introductory, first-year undergraduate, no prior RF background)
4	**Class length:** 50 minutes
5	**Prerequisites:** high-school algebra and logarithms
6	
7	## Learning objectives
8	
9	By the end of this module students can:
10	
11	1. Explain what a radio wave is and convert between frequency and wavelength.
12	2. Work in decibels: convert between watts, milliwatts and dBm, and add gains and losses.
13	3. Calculate free-space path loss and a simple link budget.
14	4. Describe how real environments (reflection, multipath, fading) change a signal.
15	5. Explain how bits are put onto a carrier (modulation) and why data rate is limited (Shannon).
16	6. Explain how many users share the spectrum (multiple access, duplexing, cells) and who regulates it.
17	
18	---
19	
20	## 1. Why wireless matters
21	
22	- A wireless link replaces a cable with an electromagnetic wave travelling through space.
23	- Everyday examples: Wi-Fi, cellular (4G/5G), Bluetooth, GPS, broadcast radio and TV, RFID tags, satellite links.
24	- Every one of these systems answers the same three questions, which structure this module:
25	  1. **How far** can the signal go? (propagation, path loss, link budget)
26	  2. **How fast** can we send data? (modulation, bandwidth, noise)
27	  3. **How many** users can share the air? (multiple access, cells, regulation)
28	
29	## 2. A short history
30	
31	| Year | Milestone |
32	|---|---|
33	| 1865 | James Clerk Maxwell publishes the equations predicting electromagnetic waves |
34	| 1886–1888 | Heinrich Hertz generates and detects radio waves in the lab |
35	| 1901 | Guglielmo Marconi receives a transatlantic radio signal |
36	| 1979–1983 | First-generation (1G) analog cellular networks (Tokyo 1979, AMPS in the US 1983) |
37	| 1991 | First GSM (2G, digital) call, in Finland |
38	| 1997 | First IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) standard |
39	| 1999 | Bluetooth 1.0 specification |
40	| 2009 | First commercial 4G LTE network (Stockholm and Oslo) |
41	| 2019 | First commercial 5G networks |
42	
43	Takeaway: about 120 years from equations to a phone in every pocket; each generation mainly changed *how efficiently* the same spectrum is used.
44	
45	## 3. Radio waves: frequency and wavelength
46	
47	- A radio wave is an oscillating electric and magnetic field that travels at the speed of light, **c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s**.
48	- **Frequency (f)**: oscillations per second, in hertz (Hz).
49	- **Wavelength (λ)**: distance between two peaks, in metres.
50	- They are linked by **λ = c / f**.
51	
52	Worked examples:
53	
54	| Frequency | Use | Wavelength |
55	|---|---|---|
56	| 100 MHz | FM radio | 3 m |
57	| 900 MHz | cellular | 33 cm |
58	| 2.4 GHz | Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, microwave ovens | 12.5 cm |
59	| 5 GHz | Wi-Fi | 6 cm |
60	| 28 GHz | 5G millimetre wave | about 1.07 cm |
61	
62	Why it matters: antenna size scales with wavelength (a quarter-wave antenna at 2.4 GHz is about 3.1 cm), and higher frequencies lose more energy and are blocked more easily by walls, bodies and rain.
63	
64	## 4. The radio spectrum
65	
66	The ITU divides the radio spectrum (3 kHz to 300 GHz) into bands:
67	
68	| Band | Range | Example uses |
69	|---|---|---|
70	| VLF | 3–30 kHz | submarine communication |
71	| LF | 30–300 kHz | navigation beacons |
72	| MF | 300 kHz–3 MHz | AM radio |
73	| HF | 3–30 MHz | shortwave, amateur radio |
74	| VHF | 30–300 MHz | FM radio, TV, air-band |
75	| UHF | 300 MHz–3 GHz | cellular, Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz, Bluetooth, GPS |
76	| SHF | 3–30 GHz | Wi-Fi 5/6 GHz, satellite, radar |
77	| EHF | 30–300 GHz | millimetre-wave 5G, radar |
78	
79	Trade-off to remember: **low frequencies travel far and penetrate buildings but carry little bandwidth; high frequencies carry lots of bandwidth but travel short distances.**
80	
81	## 5. Decibels: the language of wireless
82	
83	Signal powers in a link range over many orders of magnitude (a transmitter at 1 W, a receiver at 0.000000001 mW), so engineers use a logarithmic scale.
84	
85	- Ratio in decibels: **dB = 10 · log₁₀(P₂ / P₁)**
86	- Absolute power relative to 1 milliwatt: **dBm = 10 · log₁₀(P / 1 mW)**
87	- Antenna gain relative to an ideal isotropic antenna: **dBi**
88	
89	| Power | dBm |
90	|---|---|
91	| 1 W | 30 dBm |
92	| 100 mW | 20 dBm |
93	| 1 mW | 0 dBm |
94	| 1 µW | −30 dBm |
95	| 1 pW | −90 dBm |
96	
97	Rules of thumb:
98	
99	- +3 dB ≈ double the power; −3 dB ≈ half.
100	- +10 dB = 10 times the power; −10 dB = one tenth.
101	- In dB, gains and losses **add and subtract** instead of multiplying — this is why link budgets are easy.
102	
103	## 6. Antennas
104	
105	- An antenna converts electrical current into a radio wave (transmit) and back (receive); the same antenna works both ways.
106	- The **isotropic antenna** radiates equally in all directions; it is a theoretical reference (0 dBi).
107	- A **half-wave dipole** has a gain of 2.15 dBi.
108	- Gain does not create energy: a directional antenna (Yagi, patch, dish) **focuses** the same power into a narrower beam. More gain = narrower beamwidth.
109	- Omnidirectional antennas suit phones and home routers; directional antennas suit point-to-point links and base-station sectors.
110	- Modern systems use antenna arrays (MIMO, beamforming) to steer beams electronically.
111	
112	## 7. Propagation: free-space path loss
113	
114	Even in empty space, power spreads over a growing sphere, so received power falls with distance.
115	
116	**Free-space path loss (FSPL), with d in km and f in MHz:**
117	
118	> FSPL (dB) = 20 · log₁₀(d) + 20 · log₁₀(f) + 32.44
119	
120	Worked example — Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz over 100 m:
121	
122	- 20 · log₁₀(0.1) = −20.0
123	- 20 · log₁₀(2400) = 67.6
124	- FSPL = −20.0 + 67.6 + 32.44 ≈ **80 dB**
125	
126	Rules of thumb:
127	
128	- Doubling the distance adds about 6 dB of loss.
129	- Doubling the frequency also adds about 6 dB of loss.
130	
131	## 8. Propagation in the real world
132	
133	Real environments are not free space. A signal can be:
134	
135	- **Reflected** by large flat surfaces (buildings, the ground, walls).
136	- **Diffracted** around edges (rooftops, corners), which lets signals reach "shadowed" areas.
137	- **Scattered** by objects smaller than a wavelength (foliage, street signs).
138	- **Absorbed** by materials (concrete, water, human bodies).
139	
140	Path loss grows with distance as dⁿ, where n is the **path-loss exponent**:
141	
142	| Environment | Path-loss exponent n |
143	|---|---|
144	| Free space | 2 |
145	| Urban cellular | 2.7–3.5 |
146	| Shadowed urban cellular | 3–5 |
147	| In building, line of sight | 1.6–1.8 |
148	| In building, obstructed | 4–6 |
149	
150	## 9. Multipath and fading
151	
152	- Because of reflections, the receiver gets **several copies** of the signal arriving at slightly different times (**multipath**).
153	- The copies add up in phase (stronger) or out of phase (weaker), so signal strength can drop sharply when the receiver moves just half a wavelength — at 2.4 GHz, about 6 cm. This is **fast (small-scale) fading**.
154	- **Slow fading (shadowing)**: large obstacles such as buildings or hills cause slower changes over tens of metres.
155	- **Delay spread**: if echoes arrive spread out in time, symbols overlap (inter-symbol interference).
156	- **Doppler shift**: motion changes the received frequency by f_d = v / λ. Example: a car at 30 m/s (108 km/h) receiving a 2 GHz signal (λ = 0.15 m) sees up to 200 Hz shift.
157	- Defences: diversity (several antennas), MIMO, error-correcting codes, and OFDM (Section 12).
158	
159	## 10. Link budget
160	
161	A link budget adds up every gain and loss between transmitter and receiver:
162	
163	> P_received (dBm) = P_transmit (dBm) + G_transmit (dBi) + G_receive (dBi) − Losses (dB)
164	
165	Worked example (Wi-Fi, 100 m, free space):
166	
167	| Item | Value |
168	|---|---|
169	| Transmit power | +20 dBm (100 mW) |
170	| Transmit antenna gain | +2 dBi |
171	| Receive antenna gain | +2 dBi |
172	| Free-space path loss | −80 dB |
173	| **Received power** | **−56 dBm** |
174	
175	If the receiver needs at least −90 dBm (its **sensitivity**; example value), the **link margin** is −56 − (−90) = **34 dB**. The margin absorbs walls, fading and bad days. A link with no margin will drop out.
176	
177	## 11. Modulation: putting bits on a wave
178	
179	A pure carrier wave carries no information; we **modulate** it by changing one of its properties:
180	
181	- **Amplitude** — AM (analog), ASK (digital)
182	- **Frequency** — FM (analog), FSK (digital)
183	- **Phase** — PSK (digital)
184	- **Amplitude and phase together** — QAM (digital)
185	
186	Each distinct symbol carries a number of bits, log₂(number of points in the constellation):
187	
188	| Scheme | Points | Bits per symbol |
189	|---|---|---|
190	| BPSK | 2 | 1 |
191	| QPSK | 4 | 2 |
192	| 16-QAM | 16 | 4 |
193	| 64-QAM | 64 | 6 |
194	| 256-QAM | 256 | 8 |
195	| 1024-QAM (Wi-Fi 6) | 1024 | 10 |
196	| 4096-QAM (Wi-Fi 7) | 4096 | 12 |
197	
198	The catch: denser constellations put points closer together, so they need a cleaner signal (higher SNR). Modern radios use **adaptive modulation** — 256-QAM near the router, BPSK or QPSK at the edge of coverage.
199	
200	## 12. Bandwidth, noise and the Shannon limit
201	
202	- **Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)**: how much stronger the signal is than the background noise, usually in dB.
203	- **Shannon–Hartley theorem** — the maximum error-free data rate of a channel:
204	
205	> C = B · log₂(1 + SNR)   (C in bit/s, B in Hz, SNR as a linear ratio)
206	
207	Worked example: a 20 MHz Wi-Fi channel with SNR = 30 dB (a ratio of 1000):
208	C = 20 × 10⁶ · log₂(1001) ≈ 20 × 10⁶ × 9.97 ≈ **199 Mbit/s** per spatial stream (theoretical ceiling).
209	
210	Two levers for more speed: **more bandwidth** (rate grows linearly) or **more SNR** (rate grows only logarithmically). This is why new standards keep adding spectrum (wider channels, new bands) and antennas (MIMO adds parallel streams).
211	
212	**OFDM** splits a wide channel into many narrow subcarriers, each modulated slowly; this makes it robust to multipath. Wi-Fi (since 802.11a/g), 4G LTE and 5G NR all use OFDM.
213	
214	## 13. Sharing the air: multiple access and duplexing
215	
216	**Multiple access** — how many users share a channel:
217	
218	| Technique | Users are separated by | Example system |
219	|---|---|---|
220	| FDMA | frequency | 1G AMPS |
221	| TDMA | time slot | 2G GSM (8 time slots per 200 kHz carrier) |
222	| CDMA | code | 3G UMTS (WCDMA), IS-95 |
223	| OFDMA | groups of subcarriers and time | 4G LTE, 5G NR, Wi-Fi 6 |
224	
225	**Duplexing** — how one device both sends and receives:
226	
227	- **FDD (frequency-division duplex)**: separate frequencies for uplink and downlink, at the same time.
228	- **TDD (time-division duplex)**: the same frequency, taking turns in time; easy to shift capacity between uplink and downlink.
229	
230	**Wi-Fi** shares the channel differently: devices listen before talking (CSMA/CA) and back off if the channel is busy.
231	
232	## 14. The cellular concept
233	
234	- Instead of one powerful tower covering a city, divide the area into many small **cells**, each with a low-power base station.
235	- **Frequency reuse**: cells far enough apart can reuse the same frequencies, multiplying total capacity.
236	- **Handover**: as a user moves, the call or data session passes from one cell to the next without dropping.
237	- Smaller cells = more reuse = more capacity; this is why dense cities use small cells and 5G millimetre-wave sites.
238	
239	## 15. Who controls the spectrum
240	
241	- Spectrum is a limited, shared public resource, so it is regulated.
242	- **ITU** (International Telecommunication Union) coordinates globally; national regulators allocate locally, e.g. the **FCC** (United States) and **Ofcom** (United Kingdom).
243	- **Licensed spectrum**: an operator buys exclusive rights (often at auction) — cellular networks. Predictable, interference-managed.
244	- **Unlicensed spectrum**: anyone may transmit if they follow power rules — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, many IoT devices. Free, but shared and congested.
245	- The **2.4 GHz ISM band** (2.400–2.4835 GHz) is used by Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and microwave ovens.
246	- In 2020 the FCC opened 1,200 MHz of the 6 GHz band (5.925–7.125 GHz) for unlicensed use, used by Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7.
247	
248	## 16. Putting it together: comparing common systems
249	
250	| System | Typical bands | Typical range | Spectrum |
251	|---|---|---|---|
252	| Bluetooth | 2.4 GHz | about 10 m (typical) | unlicensed |
253	| Wi-Fi | 2.4, 5, 6 GHz | tens of metres indoors | unlicensed |
254	| 4G LTE | 600 MHz – 2.6 GHz (varies by country) | hundreds of metres to kilometres | licensed |
255	| 5G mid-band | about 3.5 GHz | hundreds of metres | licensed |
256	| 5G mmWave | 24–40 GHz | about 100–300 m, line of sight | licensed |
257	
258	Each row is the same physics from this module: frequency sets range and penetration, bandwidth and SNR set speed, and the access scheme and licensing set how many can share.
259	
260	## 17. Summary
261	
262	1. Radio waves: λ = c / f; higher frequency = smaller antennas, more bandwidth, shorter range.
263	2. Decibels turn multiplication into addition; 0 dBm = 1 mW, +3 dB ≈ ×2, +10 dB = ×10.
264	3. FSPL ≈ 80 dB for 100 m at 2.4 GHz; each doubling of distance adds 6 dB.
265	4. Real channels reflect, diffract, scatter and fade; multipath is the main enemy.
266	5. Link budget: P_r = P_t + G_t + G_r − L; keep a margin.
267	6. Modulation packs bits per symbol; denser constellations need more SNR.
268	7. Shannon: C = B · log₂(1 + SNR) — bandwidth is the strongest lever.
269	8. FDMA → TDMA → CDMA → OFDMA; FDD vs TDD; cells reuse frequencies.
270	9. Regulators split spectrum into licensed and unlicensed bands.
271	
272	**Next module (Module 2):** Antennas and propagation in depth — radiation patterns, MIMO and beamforming.
273	
274	## 18. Check your understanding (quiz)
275	
276	1. What is the wavelength of a 5 GHz signal? *(Answer: 6 cm)*
277	2. Convert 100 mW to dBm. *(Answer: 20 dBm)*
278	3. A link has 70 dB of path loss at 50 m. Roughly how much is it at 100 m in free space? *(Answer: about 76 dB)*
279	4. Which carries more bits per symbol, QPSK or 64-QAM, and what does it cost? *(Answer: 64-QAM, 6 vs 2 bits; it needs a higher SNR)*
280	5. Using Shannon, which raises capacity more: doubling bandwidth or doubling SNR at high SNR? *(Answer: doubling bandwidth)*
281	6. Name the multiple-access technique used by 4G and 5G. *(Answer: OFDMA)*
282	
283	## Glossary
284	
285	- **Carrier** — the unmodulated radio wave that carries the signal.
286	- **dBm** — power in decibels relative to 1 milliwatt.
287	- **dBi** — antenna gain relative to an isotropic antenna.
288	- **FSPL** — free-space path loss.
289	- **Link margin** — received power minus receiver sensitivity.
290	- **MIMO** — multiple-input multiple-output; several antennas on each end.
291	- **OFDM / OFDMA** — orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing / multiple access.
292	- **SNR** — signal-to-noise ratio.
293

# Wireless 101 — Module 1: How Wireless Communication Works

**Course:** Wireless 101 (introductory, first-year undergraduate, no prior RF background)
**Class length:** 50 minutes
**Prerequisites:** high-school algebra and logarithms

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module students can:

1. Explain what a radio wave is and convert between frequency and wavelength.
2. Work in decibels: convert between watts, milliwatts and dBm, and add gains and losses.
3. Calculate free-space path loss and a simple link budget.
4. Describe how real environments (reflection, multipath, fading) change a signal.
5. Explain how bits are put onto a carrier (modulation) and why data rate is limited (Shannon).
6. Explain how many users share the spectrum (multiple access, duplexing, cells) and who regulates it.

---

## 1. Why wireless matters

- A wireless link replaces a cable with an electromagnetic wave travelling through space.
- Everyday examples: Wi-Fi, cellular (4G/5G), Bluetooth, GPS, broadcast radio and TV, RFID tags, satellite links.
- Every one of these systems answers the same three questions, which structure this module:
  1. **How far** can the signal go? (propagation, path loss, link budget)
  2. **How fast** can we send data? (modulation, bandwidth, noise)
  3. **How many** users can share the air? (multiple access, cells, regulation)

## 2. A short history

| Year | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 1865 | James Clerk Maxwell publishes the equations predicting electromagnetic waves |
| 1886–1888 | Heinrich Hertz generates and detects radio waves in the lab |
| 1901 | Guglielmo Marconi receives a transatlantic radio signal |
| 1979–1983 | First-generation (1G) analog cellular networks (Tokyo 1979, AMPS in the US 1983) |
| 1991 | First GSM (2G, digital) call, in Finland |
| 1997 | First IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) standard |
| 1999 | Bluetooth 1.0 specification |
| 2009 | First commercial 4G LTE network (Stockholm and Oslo) |
| 2019 | First commercial 5G networks |

Takeaway: about 120 years from equations to a phone in every pocket; each generation mainly changed *how efficiently* the same spectrum is used.

## 3. Radio waves: frequency and wavelength

- A radio wave is an oscillating electric and magnetic field that travels at the speed of light, **c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s**.
- **Frequency (f)**: oscillations per second, in hertz (Hz).
- **Wavelength (λ)**: distance between two peaks, in metres.
- They are linked by **λ = c / f**.

Worked examples:

| Frequency | Use | Wavelength |
|---|---|---|
| 100 MHz | FM radio | 3 m |
| 900 MHz | cellular | 33 cm |
| 2.4 GHz | Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, microwave ovens | 12.5 cm |
| 5 GHz | Wi-Fi | 6 cm |
| 28 GHz | 5G millimetre wave | about 1.07 cm |

## 4. The radio spectrum

The ITU divides the radio spectrum (3 kHz to 300 GHz) into bands:

| Band | Range | Example uses |
|---|---|---|
| VLF | 3–30 kHz | submarine communication |
| LF | 30–300 kHz | navigation beacons |
| MF | 300 kHz–3 MHz | AM radio |
| HF | 3–30 MHz | shortwave, amateur radio |
| VHF | 30–300 MHz | FM radio, TV, air-band |
| UHF | 300 MHz–3 GHz | cellular, Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz, Bluetooth, GPS |
| SHF | 3–30 GHz | Wi-Fi 5/6 GHz, satellite, radar |
| EHF | 30–300 GHz | millimetre-wave 5G, radar |

## 5. Decibels: the language of wireless

Signal powers in a link range over many orders of magnitude (a transmitter at 1 W, a receiver at 0.000000001 mW), so engineers use a logarithmic scale.

- Ratio in decibels: **dB = 10 · log₁₀(P₂ / P₁)**
- Absolute power relative to 1 milliwatt: **dBm = 10 · log₁₀(P / 1 mW)**
- Antenna gain relative to an ideal isotropic antenna: **dBi**

| Power | dBm |
|---|---|
| 1 W | 30 dBm |
| 100 mW | 20 dBm |
| 1 mW | 0 dBm |
| 1 µW | −30 dBm |
| 1 pW | −90 dBm |

Rules of thumb:

- +3 dB ≈ double the power; −3 dB ≈ half.
- +10 dB = 10 times the power; −10 dB = one tenth.
- In dB, gains and losses **add and subtract** instead of multiplying — this is why link budgets are easy.

## 6. Antennas

- An antenna converts electrical current into a radio wave (transmit) and back (receive); the same antenna works both ways.
- The **isotropic antenna** radiates equally in all directions; it is a theoretical reference (0 dBi).
- A **half-wave dipole** has a gain of 2.15 dBi.
- Gain does not create energy: a directional antenna (Yagi, patch, dish) **focuses** the same power into a narrower beam. More gain = narrower beamwidth.
- Omnidirectional antennas suit phones and home routers; directional antennas suit point-to-point links and base-station sectors.
- Modern systems use antenna arrays (MIMO, beamforming) to steer beams electronically.

## 7. Propagation: free-space path loss

Even in empty space, power spreads over a growing sphere, so received power falls with distance.

**Free-space path loss (FSPL), with d in km and f in MHz:**

> FSPL (dB) = 20 · log₁₀(d) + 20 · log₁₀(f) + 32.44

Worked example — Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz over 100 m:

- 20 · log₁₀(0.1) = −20.0
- 20 · log₁₀(2400) = 67.6
- FSPL = −20.0 + 67.6 + 32.44 ≈ **80 dB**

Rules of thumb:

- Doubling the distance adds about 6 dB of loss.
- Doubling the frequency also adds about 6 dB of loss.

## 8. Propagation in the real world

Real environments are not free space. A signal can be:

- **Reflected** by large flat surfaces (buildings, the ground, walls).
- **Diffracted** around edges (rooftops, corners), which lets signals reach "shadowed" areas.
- **Scattered** by objects smaller than a wavelength (foliage, street signs).
- **Absorbed** by materials (concrete, water, human bodies).

Path loss grows with distance as dⁿ, where n is the **path-loss exponent**:

| Environment | Path-loss exponent n |
|---|---|
| Free space | 2 |
| Urban cellular | 2.7–3.5 |
| Shadowed urban cellular | 3–5 |
| In building, line of sight | 1.6–1.8 |
| In building, obstructed | 4–6 |

## 9. Multipath and fading

- Because of reflections, the receiver gets **several copies** of the signal arriving at slightly different times (**multipath**).
- The copies add up in phase (stronger) or out of phase (weaker), so signal strength can drop sharply when the receiver moves just half a wavelength — at 2.4 GHz, about 6 cm. This is **fast (small-scale) fading**.
- **Slow fading (shadowing)**: large obstacles such as buildings or hills cause slower changes over tens of metres.
- **Delay spread**: if echoes arrive spread out in time, symbols overlap (inter-symbol interference).
- **Doppler shift**: motion changes the received frequency by f_d = v / λ. Example: a car at 30 m/s (108 km/h) receiving a 2 GHz signal (λ = 0.15 m) sees up to 200 Hz shift.
- Defences: diversity (several antennas), MIMO, error-correcting codes, and OFDM (Section 12).

## 10. Link budget

A link budget adds up every gain and loss between transmitter and receiver:

> P_received (dBm) = P_transmit (dBm) + G_transmit (dBi) + G_receive (dBi) − Losses (dB)

Worked example (Wi-Fi, 100 m, free space):

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Transmit power | +20 dBm (100 mW) |
| Transmit antenna gain | +2 dBi |
| Receive antenna gain | +2 dBi |
| Free-space path loss | −80 dB |
| **Received power** | **−56 dBm** |

If the receiver needs at least −90 dBm (its **sensitivity**; example value), the **link margin** is −56 − (−90) = **34 dB**. The margin absorbs walls, fading and bad days. A link with no margin will drop out.

## 11. Modulation: putting bits on a wave

A pure carrier wave carries no information; we **modulate** it by changing one of its properties:

- **Amplitude** — AM (analog), ASK (digital)
- **Frequency** — FM (analog), FSK (digital)
- **Phase** — PSK (digital)
- **Amplitude and phase together** — QAM (digital)

Each distinct symbol carries a number of bits, log₂(number of points in the constellation):

| Scheme | Points | Bits per symbol |
|---|---|---|
| BPSK | 2 | 1 |
| QPSK | 4 | 2 |
| 16-QAM | 16 | 4 |
| 64-QAM | 64 | 6 |
| 256-QAM | 256 | 8 |
| 1024-QAM (Wi-Fi 6) | 1024 | 10 |
| 4096-QAM (Wi-Fi 7) | 4096 | 12 |

The catch: denser constellations put points closer together, so they need a cleaner signal (higher SNR). Modern radios use **adaptive modulation** — 256-QAM near the router, BPSK or QPSK at the edge of coverage.

## 12. Bandwidth, noise and the Shannon limit

- **Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)**: how much stronger the signal is than the background noise, usually in dB.
- **Shannon–Hartley theorem** — the maximum error-free data rate of a channel:

> C = B · log₂(1 + SNR)   (C in bit/s, B in Hz, SNR as a linear ratio)

Worked example: a 20 MHz Wi-Fi channel with SNR = 30 dB (a ratio of 1000):
C = 20 × 10⁶ · log₂(1001) ≈ 20 × 10⁶ × 9.97 ≈ **199 Mbit/s** per spatial stream (theoretical ceiling).

Two levers for more speed: **more bandwidth** (rate grows linearly) or **more SNR** (rate grows only logarithmically). This is why new standards keep adding spectrum (wider channels, new bands) and antennas (MIMO adds parallel streams).

**OFDM** splits a wide channel into many narrow subcarriers, each modulated slowly; this makes it robust to multipath. Wi-Fi (since 802.11a/g), 4G LTE and 5G NR all use OFDM.

## 13. Sharing the air: multiple access and duplexing

**Multiple access** — how many users share a channel:

| Technique | Users are separated by | Example system |
|---|---|---|
| FDMA | frequency | 1G AMPS |
| TDMA | time slot | 2G GSM (8 time slots per 200 kHz carrier) |
| CDMA | code | 3G UMTS (WCDMA), IS-95 |
| OFDMA | groups of subcarriers and time | 4G LTE, 5G NR, Wi-Fi 6 |

**Duplexing** — how one device both sends and receives:

- **FDD (frequency-division duplex)**: separate frequencies for uplink and downlink, at the same time.
- **TDD (time-division duplex)**: the same frequency, taking turns in time; easy to shift capacity between uplink and downlink.

**Wi-Fi** shares the channel differently: devices listen before talking (CSMA/CA) and back off if the channel is busy.

## 14. The cellular concept

- Instead of one powerful tower covering a city, divide the area into many small **cells**, each with a low-power base station.
- **Frequency reuse**: cells far enough apart can reuse the same frequencies, multiplying total capacity.
- **Handover**: as a user moves, the call or data session passes from one cell to the next without dropping.
- Smaller cells = more reuse = more capacity; this is why dense cities use small cells and 5G millimetre-wave sites.

## 15. Who controls the spectrum

- Spectrum is a limited, shared public resource, so it is regulated.
- **ITU** (International Telecommunication Union) coordinates globally; national regulators allocate locally, e.g. the **FCC** (United States) and **Ofcom** (United Kingdom).
- **Licensed spectrum**: an operator buys exclusive rights (often at auction) — cellular networks. Predictable, interference-managed.
- **Unlicensed spectrum**: anyone may transmit if they follow power rules — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, many IoT devices. Free, but shared and congested.
- The **2.4 GHz ISM band** (2.400–2.4835 GHz) is used by Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and microwave ovens.
- In 2020 the FCC opened 1,200 MHz of the 6 GHz band (5.925–7.125 GHz) for unlicensed use, used by Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7.

## 16. Putting it together: comparing common systems

| System | Typical bands | Typical range | Spectrum |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bluetooth | 2.4 GHz | about 10 m (typical) | unlicensed |
| Wi-Fi | 2.4, 5, 6 GHz | tens of metres indoors | unlicensed |
| 4G LTE | 600 MHz – 2.6 GHz (varies by country) | hundreds of metres to kilometres | licensed |
| 5G mid-band | about 3.5 GHz | hundreds of metres | licensed |
| 5G mmWave | 24–40 GHz | about 100–300 m, line of sight | licensed |

Each row is the same physics from this module: frequency sets range and penetration, bandwidth and SNR set speed, and the access scheme and licensing set how many can share.

## 17. Summary

1. Radio waves: λ = c / f; higher frequency = smaller antennas, more bandwidth, shorter range.
2. Decibels turn multiplication into addition; 0 dBm = 1 mW, +3 dB ≈ ×2, +10 dB = ×10.
3. FSPL ≈ 80 dB for 100 m at 2.4 GHz; each doubling of distance adds 6 dB.
4. Real channels reflect, diffract, scatter and fade; multipath is the main enemy.
5. Link budget: P_r = P_t + G_t + G_r − L; keep a margin.
6. Modulation packs bits per symbol; denser constellations need more SNR.
7. Shannon: C = B · log₂(1 + SNR) — bandwidth is the strongest lever.
8. FDMA → TDMA → CDMA → OFDMA; FDD vs TDD; cells reuse frequencies.
9. Regulators split spectrum into licensed and unlicensed bands.

**Next module (Module 2):** Antennas and propagation in depth — radiation patterns, MIMO and beamforming.

## 18. Check your understanding (quiz)

1. What is the wavelength of a 5 GHz signal? *(Answer: 6 cm)*
2. Convert 100 mW to dBm. *(Answer: 20 dBm)*
3. A link has 70 dB of path loss at 50 m. Roughly how much is it at 100 m in free space? *(Answer: about 76 dB)*
4. Which carries more bits per symbol, QPSK or 64-QAM, and what does it cost? *(Answer: 64-QAM, 6 vs 2 bits; it needs a higher SNR)*
5. Using Shannon, which raises capacity more: doubling bandwidth or doubling SNR at high SNR? *(Answer: doubling bandwidth)*
6. Name the multiple-access technique used by 4G and 5G. *(Answer: OFDMA)*

## Glossary

- **Carrier** — the unmodulated radio wave that carries the signal.
- **dBm** — power in decibels relative to 1 milliwatt.
- **dBi** — antenna gain relative to an isotropic antenna.
- **FSPL** — free-space path loss.
- **Link margin** — received power minus receiver sensitivity.
- **MIMO** — multiple-input multiple-output; several antennas on each end.
- **OFDM / OFDMA** — orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing / multiple access.
- **SNR** — signal-to-noise ratio.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/hishamabuella/Work/Presentation_Claude_SKILL/keynote_html_claude_skill/plugins/present-in-html/skills/present-in-html

# Presentations as one HTML file

The deck engine (Keynote Pro) is a single HTML file: a fixed 16:9 stage, 32 themes, auto-fitting type, builds, Magic Move,
charts from data, a presenter window, a link to every slide and PDF printing. No framework or build step; the deck opens from
`file://`. You write plain HTML slides into a copy of the template.

**Part of the deck workflow** (plan, build, review, publish; the `deck-workflow` skill runs it end to end). This skill
covers planning (sections 1 to 5, the outline in `PLAN.md`) and building (section 6). A user can enter the workflow here,
or anywhere later: with a `PLAN.md` it starts at the build, with a finished deck at the review.

```bash
S=<skill base dir>        # shown when this skill loads
```

Treat `$S` as read-only: copy the template into the user's folder and work on the copy, so the skill stays reusable.

| File | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `assets/template.html` | the starting point; every layout once as a sample slide, so it is also the markup to copy |
| `assets/library/` | profession themes and font pairings that `add-look.mjs` copies into a deck |
| `assets/examples/beyond-slides.html` | model deck for live demos on slides (app UI, simulation, sound, code, video) |
| `scripts/check.mjs` | the checker (overflow, text size, contrast, missing notes) and `--shots`, `--outline` |
| `scripts/add-look.mjs` | copies a library theme or font pairing into a deck |
| `scripts/assemble.mjs` | joins slide parts written in parallel into one deck |
| `scripts/upgrade.mjs` | moves a deck made with an older engine onto the current one |
| `references/looks.md` | every theme, font pairing, layout and feature on one page: read it to pick the look |
| `references/manual.md` | the engine manual; section 2 is the layout cheat-sheet with markup for every layout |
| `references/outline.md` | the `PLAN.md` format: the outline every deck is built from |
| `references/engine.md` | slide links, live demos, narration, the `window.kp` API, slide attributes |

## 1. Start from the user's material

Most decks start from something: a topic, an outline, notes, a document, a spreadsheet, a link. Read all of it before
planning, because the deck's credibility comes from using the user's real facts, not plausible-sounding ones.

- **Files** (PDF, Word, Markdown, text, slides to redo): read them fully; pull out the claims, numbers, names, dates and quotes.
- **Data** (CSV, Excel, JSON, a table in the message): compute what the story needs (totals, growth, shares) and keep the
  figures exact. Charts take `data-values="Q1:12,Q2:18"` or a `<table>` for several series.
- **Links**: fetch them and use what they say; cite them in the notes or a `references` slide.
- **An outline**: keep the user's order and headings; your job is to turn each heading into a claim and pick its layout.
- **Only a topic**: write the outline yourself from what you know, and mark anything the user should verify.

Never invent numbers, names, quotes or sources: a wrong number on a slide damages the presenter in front of their audience.
Where data is missing, use a clearly labelled placeholder ("illustrative", "TBC") and list the placeholders when you deliver.

## 2. Ask little, decide the rest

Ask only what you cannot know or find in the material: (1) audience and occasion (who, how long), (2) the facts they want
shown, if none were given. Decide everything else: theme, fonts, recipe, slide count (about one per minute; 1.5 to 2 for a
lecture), builds. State the choice in one line, e.g. "Boardroom theme, board-review recipe, 11 slides, count-up on the KPIs",
then build. A questionnaire costs the user more than a decision they can change.

## 3. Pick the look

Read `references/looks.md` and match the need: a profession look when one fits (a lawyer gets `chambers`, a finance team
`ledger`), else a core theme by occasion (launch `keynote-black`/`keynote-white`, board `boardroom`, tech talk `swiss`,
teaching `studio`, essay or weekly update `editorial`). Each library look comes with a recipe: the layouts in a good order.

`data-theme` and `data-fonts` go on `<html>` (empty `data-fonts` = the theme's own pairing). The template carries the 6 core
themes; library themes are copied into the deck, so it stays one file:

```bash
node "$S/scripts/add-look.mjs" my-deck.html --theme ledger        # before running the checker: an unknown theme falls back to the first core one
node "$S/scripts/add-look.mjs" --list                             # every library theme and pairing
```

A brand colour is one line in the deck's `<style>`: `html{--brand:#7c3aed;--brand-text:#7c3aed}`. For a deck that must
work without internet, set `data-fonts="system"`.

## 4. Shape the talk first

Before writing slides, plan with Patrick Winston's speaking rules (MIT, "How to Speak"); review-deck later checks the same:

- **Open with a promise**, not a joke: slide 1 or 2 says what the audience will know or be able to do by the end.
- **Say the main idea three times, three ways**: early, at a section break, at the end (a metaphor, an example, a question).
- **Fence it**: one line or slide on what the idea is *not*, against the nearest alternative.
- **Signpost** a longer talk: an agenda that returns, or section slides; add one real question to the audience where it fits.
- **Slides support the speaker**: few words on the slide, the why and the story in the notes, never a slide to read aloud.
  Give each key number a short story or comparison.
- **End on a contribution**: the last slide says what the audience now has, or the ask; not "Thank you" or "Questions?".
  The notes end with a salute to the audience, not thanks.

## 5. Write the outline

Write the outline to `PLAN.md` next to the deck in the format in `references/outline.md`: promise, story, fence, look, then
one row per slide with its layout, its claim (the slide's `<h2>`), the facts it uses with their source, its role (promise,
signpost, thesis, fence, evidence, story, question, contribution) and its minutes. The roles make the rules above
concrete, and the minutes show whether it fits the slot before any slide exists.

Show the user the outline table with the one-line look choice, then build. Wait for their OK first only if they asked to
see the plan, or the deck is long (over about 15 slides), where rework is costly.

## 6. Build it

```bash
cp "$S/assets/template.html" my-deck.html
# set data-theme / data-fonts / lang (and dir="rtl" for Arabic) on <html>; set <title> and data-title on <main class="deck">
# to the same text; delete every sample slide between SLIDES:START and SLIDES:END
```

1. Follow `PLAN.md` slide by slide: its order, `data-id`s, layouts and claims as the `<h2>`s. Reading only the titles in
   order should tell the whole argument.
2. For each slide add the layout's markup from `references/manual.md` section 2, and `<aside class="notes">` with what to say and
   where the numbers come from. The notes are the speaker's script and the presenter window shows them.
3. Check, fix, check again:
   ```bash
   node "$S/scripts/check.mjs" my-deck.html              # fix every error; it prints "slide n: element, problem, fix:"
   node "$S/scripts/check.mjs" my-deck.html --themes     # same checks in every theme in the deck (someone will press S)
   node "$S/scripts/check.mjs" my-deck.html --shots shots/   # PNG per slide: look at the title, a chart, the densest slide, the close
   ```
   Fix the cause the checker names; when text overflows, cut words or split the slide rather than tuning CSS, since auto-fit
   already shrinks type to 78% and smaller text would fail the 28px floor. After three failing passes, restructure the slide.
   If Playwright is missing, the checker prints the exact install line; install it outside the skill folder
   (`mkdir -p ~/.kp-tools && cd ~/.kp-tools && npm i playwright && npx playwright install chromium`).
4. Compare the built deck with the plan: `node "$S/scripts/check.mjs" my-deck.html --outline` lists every slide's title
   and layout; it should match `PLAN.md` row for row.

### Large decks: write parts in parallel, assemble at the end

Past about 15 slides, one pass gets slow and uneven. Split the `PLAN.md` rows into parts of 4 to 8 slides. Then spawn one
subagent per part in a single message. Each gets the plan, its part, `references/manual.md` section 2 and the template, and writes only
`<section class="slide">` elements (with notes) to `parts/NN-name.html`, using only the facts given. Then:

```bash
node "$S/scripts/assemble.mjs" my-deck.html parts/*.html --theme ledger --title "Q3 review"   # [--lang ar --dir rtl]
node "$S/scripts/check.mjs" my-deck.html --shots shots/
```

Read the assembled deck start to end yourself: one voice, no repeated points, numbers that agree across parts.

## 7. Quality bar

- One idea per slide; the `<h2>` is the claim ("Revenue grew 18%"), not the topic ("Revenue"). At most 5 short bullets.
- Vary layouts: no more than two bullet slides in a row; a section break every 3 to 5 slides in a long deck.
- Motion has a job: a build reveals the next point, `count` lands a number, Magic Move links the same object across slides,
  `draw` shows a trend forming. No decorative motion, emoji icons or second accent colour; they make a deck look generated.
- Charts carry the takeaway in `.lede`, a source in `<figcaption>`, and `data-highlight` on the bar that matters.

## 8. Arabic and RTL

`<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">` (or `dir="rtl"` on one `<section>` in a mixed deck) mirrors every layout. Translate `<title>`,
`data-title` and the footer too, since the footer shows on every slide. Keep code in `dir="ltr"` and Latin brand names as they
are. Write Egyptian or Modern Standard Arabic as the user asks. For bilingual decks use the `trainer` look. Check the screenshots:
headings, timelines and chart labels must read right to left.

## 9. Deliver

Tell the user briefly: the file path; open it in Chrome and press **F** for fullscreen; **P** presenter window (notes, next
slide, timer), **G** overview, **O** outline, **S** theme panel, **M** marker, **B** black screen, **K** copy this slide's link;
PDF via Cmd/Ctrl+P (Save as PDF, margins None, background graphics on). Add the one-line look choice, the placeholders still
to fill, and the checker result ("0 errors in 7 themes").

Then mention the companion skills: **deck-workflow** to plan, build, review and publish in one run, **edit-deck** to fix
wording in a click-and-type editor, **review-deck** to check the deck
against its audience and time slot, **publish-deck** to put it online on GitHub Pages.

## Layouts (`data-layout`)

| Layout | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `title` | opening slide; also `closing` for the end |
| `section` | part breaks every 3 to 5 slides |
| `statement` | one big sentence: the claim, a turn in the story |
| `agenda` | what is coming; `aria-current` marks where we are |
| `bullets` | at most 5 short points, built one by one |
| `two-column` | A vs B, before/after, risks/asks; `data-cols="3"` for three |
| `image-left` / `image-right` | a picture with a point |
| `full-bleed` | a photo with a title on it |
| `big-number` | one number that matters, counted up |
| `stats` | 2 to 4 KPIs |
| `chart` | column, bar or line from `data-values` or a table; takeaway in `.lede` |
| `comparison` | options in a table with a recommended column |
| `timeline` | dates and milestones; `class="now"` marks today |
| `process` | 3 to 5 steps |
| `quote` | a voice: customer, source, clause |
| `code` | code with focus steps per click |
| `team` | people with initials or photos |
| `diagram` | inline SVG that draws itself |
| `formula` | one equation, explained |
| `case` | a case record: summary, vitals, timed course |
| `ask` | the raise or the need: amount, use of funds, terms |
| `rows` | labelled rows: issue/rule/application/conclusion, claim/evidence/caveat |
| `quiz` | a question; the click reveals the answer |
| `materials` | a board of swatches or samples |
| `references` | sources and further reading |

Markup for each is in `references/manual.md` section 2 (the cheat-sheet).

## Features worth using

- **Builds**: `data-build="list|fade|rise|scale|wipe|count|draw"` reveal points in order, count numbers up, grow bars, draw lines; `data-focus` steps through code.
- **Backup slides**: a `data-layout="appendix"` slide (or `data-appendix`) and everything after it is skipped in play; `data-skip` skips one slide.
- **Magic Move**: the same `data-magic` id on two consecutive slides morphs the object between them.
- **Charts** from data (`data-chart` column, bar, line; multi-series from a `<table>`), with highlight, units, source.
- **Diagrams** as inline SVG that draw on entry.
- **Presenter window** (P): notes, next build, timer; `data-duration="20"` makes it a countdown.
- **Slide links** (`data-id`), overview (G), outline (O), marker (M), laser (L), theme panel (S), black screen (B).
- **Narration**: one MP3 per slide plays and advances (`data-narration`).
- **Slides that run**: live UI, calculators, simulations, sound, code, games, iframes, video, camera.
- **Arabic / RTL**: `dir="rtl"` mirrors every layout; bilingual with the `trainer` look.
- **PDF**: Cmd/Ctrl+P, one slide per page, builds shown.

# The outline (PLAN.md)

The contract between planning and building. Whoever builds the deck follows it slide by slide, and the review compares the
finished deck against it, so every field is concrete: no "TBD" except facts the user still has to supply.

## Format

```markdown
# <Deck title>

- **Audience**: who, and what they already know
- **Occasion and time**: event, slot in minutes, whether Q&A is inside the slot
- **Goal**: what the audience should know, decide or do at the end
- **Promise**: By the end you will ... (said on slide 1 or 2)
- **Story**: the whole argument in one sentence
- **Fence**: what the idea is not (the nearest alternative it could be confused with)
- **Look**: data-theme, data-fonts (empty = the theme's own), lang/dir, one line on why
- **Sources**: each file or link used, one per line
- **Placeholders**: facts still missing, or "none"

| # | data-id | layout | claim (the slide's h2) | content and facts (with source) | role | min |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | start | title | ... | subtitle = the promise | promise | 0.5 |
| 2 | agenda | agenda | ... | the parts | signpost | 0.5 |
| ... |
| n | close | closing | ... | what the audience now has, or the ask | contribution | 1 |

**Total**: n slides, about N minutes (finish at 85 to 90% of the slot when Q&A is inside it).
**Restatements of the story**: slides a, b, c (three, said three different ways).
```

## Rules for filling it in

- **Claim**: a sentence that states something ("Revenue grew 18%"), not a topic ("Revenue"). The titles alone, read in
  order, tell the story.
- **Content and facts**: only from the user's material, each with its source; anything missing is a named placeholder.
- **Role**, one or more per slide: promise, signpost, thesis (a restatement of the story), fence, evidence, story (an
  example or case that makes a number tangible), question (to the room), contribution, backup.
- **Layout**: one from `references/looks.md`; no more than two bullet slides in a row.
- **Minutes**: about one per slide for a talk, 1.5 to 2 for a lecture; the total fits the slot.
- **Required roles**: a promise in slides 1 to 2, the story restated three times, a fence, a contribution or the ask
  as the last slide (never "Thank you" or "Questions?"), and signposts when the talk is longer than about 10 minutes.
- Backup slides go last with role `backup`; they start with an appendix slide and are not counted in the time.
